sentences: If your pain has lasted months, and a doctor has checked and found no injury or disease to explain it, two therapies are worth knowing about.
In the first, Pain Reprocessing Therapy, you learn to treat the pain as a false alarm.
It's real, but it's your brain signaling danger where the doctors haven't found any injury.
Part of how you learn that is by paying close attention to how the pain feels in your body without fearing it.
Then, a little at a time, you go back to things you've been avoiding because of it, like going for walks.

fable: The paragraph runs in a very even explainer order (condition, announcement, definition, reassurance, step one, step two), each sentence carrying exactly one point at a similar medium length, with no aside, opinion or detail that only this writer would have. The steady second-person "you learn / you go back" voice is clear but neutral, which is what makes it read as polished more than as written by someone.
haiku: The paragraph is evenly balanced, with each sentence neatly set up and resolved, which gives it a polished, generic arc from condition to explanation to gradual return. Its voice is a general "you" with no specific speaker or particular detail, so it reads as produced rather than written from experience.
sonnet: The paragraph moves in even, medium-length sentences through a tidy setup, definition, reassurance and next-step order, with no digression, no rough edge and no personal voice. Every sentence has the same calm, explanatory tone.
